paper_title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Schema matching reconciles multiple database schemas by identifying semantic correspondences
between source and target schema elements through mapping techniques [19]. In conventional
approaches, similarity scores are computed for each pair of attribute names and accepted if they
exceed a predefined threshold. However, these methods often lack the depth to recognize im-
plicit semantic relationships, such as synonyms, abbreviations, and different terminologies from
heterogeneous schemas, due to their inherent reliance on surface-level similarity. This seman-
tic heterogeneity frequently necessitates human intervention and domain expertise to validate
mapping decisions [54]. Given the vast number of entities and attributes across heterogeneous
databases, such manual oversight is impractical. For example, disparate management information
systems (MIS), including electronic health records (EHR), must often be integrated into a stan-
dardized database to ensure efficient data access and management. Here is an example of schema
matching between the e-MedSolution data model [40] and the OMOP CDM data model [23] from
the real-world scenario. As shown in Figure 1, the ATTEND_DOCTOR from hun_case_i(o) table is
a semantically similar attribute with the DOCTOR of hun_case_diag table in the source schema,
and both of them should be matched with the provider_id from CONDITION_OCCURRENCE table in
the target schema. Traditional schema matching approaches struggle with such complex scenarios
due to semantic heterogeneity and ambiguity, as they do not effectively capture the semantic
information and the meaning of the tables [16].
sections.content: In recent years, language models have demonstrated superior capabilities in schema matching and heterogeneous data integration. For instance, past works propose to integrate the textual description of entities and attributes with large language models (LLMs) [51], e.g., fine-tuning LLMs [63, 83], prompting LLMs [15], and augmenting LLMs [60] to generate the top-𝑘 mappings. Other works employ pre-trained language models (PLMs) to classify the potential mappings [68, 88]. However, the SOTA LLM-based and PLM-based schema matching is still incapable of handling 2 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár Fig. 1. Example of schema matching in the EHR data model. Table (a) and Table (b) are from the source schema, and Table (c) is from the target schema. The textual description for attributes originates from the database design documents. Solid arrows indicate the corresponding mappings share the same color. the conflicts and ambiguities at the semantic level (e.g., acronyms, abbreviations, relatedness, etc.) in certain complex mapping cases, for instance, identifying the matches between ATTEND_DOCTOR and provider_id in the above example. The reasons are twofold: (1) The schema matching in real-world data integration usually involves identifying the semantic correspondence between attributes spanning across multiple tables from heterogeneous schemas; (2) LLM and PLM-based methods necessitate textual descriptions and background knowledge to analyze the given tables and attribute names; however, the background knowledge is often absent in real-world databases. Without acquiring the background knowledge, the LLM-based method could only incorporate the textual information at the syntactic level [43, 84], which limits their capabilities to detect deeper semantic correspondences and find many-to-one mappings with similar semantic meanings [4]. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are one of the widely used knowledge bases, where the rich semantic knowledge and fact-based relations are structured in the form of subject, predicate, object triples [10]. They store large-scale, real-world facts using graph structures in highly curated manner [86], where node (subject or object) represents an entity, and an edge (predicate) denotes relationship between two entities. The structured semantic knowledge in external commonsense KGs makes it possible to enhance the language models with knowledge inference by incorporating commonsense knowledge, factual knowledge, and domain knowledge, thereby resolving complex matching cases without any re-training of LLMs. In particular, commonsense, fact-based, and domain-specific KGs can be introduced to augment the LLMs and better handle the above complex schema matching case. This is mainly facilitated by the commonsense and fact-based KGs, such as Wikidata [69], which contain several common knowledge facts for taxonomic and hierarchical relationships, acronyms, abbreviations, relatedness, etc., which are always accessible and retrievable. Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching 3 Meanwhile, domain-specific KGs, such as Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) and SNOMEDCT [77], also contain rich relationships between, e.g., healthcare and medical terms, concepts, and codes with synonyms, which are useful for augmenting the LLMs to handle complex schema matching cases in the healthcare databases. Fig. 2. The effectiveness of KG context in augmenting LLMs for complex schema matching. For instance, consider the mapping between ATTEND_DOCTOR and provider_id. The retrieved information from commonsense KG can augment and guide LLMs to respond with the correct answer. As demonstrated in Figure 2, the retrieved KG context can help LLMs find the potential semantic similarity between the two attributes, which augments the capability of LLMs for complex schema matching tasks. Given that the rich fact-based semantic knowledge inherent in KGs has demonstrated remarkable performance in knowledge reasoning and semantic disambiguation [56, 75], KGs can be exploited to augment the capability of LLMs for the aforementioned complex schema matching. Unlike mainstream Graph RAG and KG-RAG for knowledge graph question answering (KGQA), where local, small-scale KGs can be built from benchmark datasets or text chunks [22, 32, 57, 58], there are no internal KGs within databases that can be directly leveraged to augment LLMs for complex schema matching because the required semantic knowledge exists in external and large KGs. It is not technically feasible to augment the LLMs with these large-scale KGs directly, because the contexts of LLMs have finite length [76]. Besides, context-poisoning issues may occur if too much irrelevant knowledge is utilized to augment the prompt. As result, the performance of the LLM-based schema matching will decrease [51]. Therefore, the key technical challenge of augmenting LLMs with external KGs lies in how to effectively and efficiently retrieve the relevant subgraphs from the large-scale external KGs, for instance, Wikidata includes billions of triples [69]. To address the above challenges, we propose Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation for Schema Matching (KG-RAG4SM). Our method integrates vector-based, LLM-based, and graph traversal-based retrievals to identify the relevant subgraphs from large and external KGs and further prunes the irrelevant knowledge by using ranking scheme. Then, it leverages the retrieved subgraphs to augment the LLMs and prompts for generating the final results for the complex schema-matching task. 4 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár Fig. 3. Overview of our proposed KG-RAG4SM method. Given schema matching questions and an external knowledge graph (KG), we (1) retrieve the relevant KG triples based on vector similarity between question embeddings and KG triple embeddings; (2) prune the retrieved relevant KG triples with vector similarity-based rankings; (3) augment prompts with the retrieved and refined subgraphs and generate the final answer for the given schema matching questions. As shown in Figure 3, we introduce novel knowledge graph retrieval and subgraph pruning techniques to retrieve and prune the relevant subgraphs from large KGs for augmenting the prompts and LLMs. Our method compares favorably with baseline models [68, 83, 85] in handling the semantic conflicts of complex mapping cases, by retrieving the relevant subgraphs from large and external KGs and reconciling them with LLMs for augmenting the schema matching. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to augment the LLMs and prompts for schema matching tasks with the retrieved relevant subgraphs from large and external KGs. Unlike the emerging Graph RAG [22, 58, 72] and KG-RAG [32, 57] that retrieve local neighbors or subgraphs from small, selfconstructed graphs out of text chunks, or the inherent KGs derived from the knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) dataset, our KG-RAG4SM retrieves relevant subgraphs directly from large external commonsense KGs. This enables the system to leverage rich factual knowledge to resolve complex cross-domain schema matching tasks. Mainstream graph reasoning methods [5, 38, 65, 90] generate multi-step paths through KG, typically via beam search or chain-of-thought prompting, which introduces significant computational overhead on large graphs and complex queries. KG-RAG4SM takes different route: it uses hybrid retrieval, knowledge refinement, and exclusion mechanisms to extract compact, task-relevant factual subgraph from large external KGs, enabling one-shot grounding rather than iterative path construction. By grounding the LLM in retrieved precise facts instead of internalizing graph thinking patterns, KG-RAG4SM delivers more efficient and accurate cross-domain schema matching performance. Our contributions are outlined as follows. We present knowledge graph-based retrieval-augmented generation for schema matching that retrieves and integrates the relevant subgraphs from large external KGs into LLM-based schema matching via in-context learning. We prune the retrieved subgraphs by removing the irrelevant entities and edges based on ranking scheme to provide concise and factual knowledge for augmenting the LLMs and address the context poisoning issue in schema matching. We conduct thorough experimental evaluation on six benchmark datasets across domains and case study from the real-world healthcare database to demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability across KG domains of our solutions. We introduce EMED, new schema matching dataset from the real-world healthcare domain. This will promote future research on domain-specific schema matching and data integration. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The preliminaries and the problem formulation are given in 2. The details of our proposed KG-RAG4SM method are introduced in 3. Then, experimental evaluation and the case study are conducted in 4, and the related work is summarized in 5. Finally, the conclusion and the future work are stated in 6. The additional empirical evaluation, ablation study, sensitivity analysis, and complexity analysis are provided in the Appendix.

2.2 Problem Statement
We formally define the problem of knowledge graph-based retrieval-augmented generation for
schema matching. Given a large language model (LLM), an external and large-scale knowledge
graph KG, a retrieved subgraph G, and a schema matching task 𝜃 , formally, the KG-RAG4SM is a
transformation F :
sections.content: LLM := (LLM, G) s.t. 𝑎LLM (𝜃 ) > 𝑎LLM(𝜃 ) where LLM denotes the LLMs augmented with the retrieved subgraph (G KG) from large-size KG. The constraint 𝑎LLM (𝜃 ) > 𝑎LLM(𝜃 ) describes that the overall correctness of the generated answers for schema matching by LLMs augmented with retrieved subgraphs is better than the answers generated by LLMs without retrieved subgraphs from the KG for schema matching. In our KG-RAG4SM, KG-RAG is introduced to augment the generation phase of LLMs for complex tasks by integrating LLM-based, vector-based, and graph traversal-based, as well as hybrid retrievals to retrieve the relevant subgraphs from large KGs. Technically, KG-RAG augments the question using the top-𝑘 subgraphs from KG based on vector similarity and ranking.

3.2.1 Retrieving Relevant Entities from the KG. Before retrieving the subgraph from KG, we need to
retrieve the entities from large-size KGs that are relevant to the given question of schema matching.
We follow one of the two developed paradigms for this purpose.
LLM-based Entity Retrieval. Given a schema-matching question, in this approach, we ask an
LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to retrieve a few relevant entities from the KG. Our prompts for this
purpose, including a few-shot examples with their correct answers and explanations, are illustrated
in Appendix A.2. The placeholders {question} are replaced with the real questions from our selected
dataset. Nevertheless, LLMs can hallucinate; thus, they may report some entities that do not, in
fact, exist in the commonsense KG. Therefore, we need to verify the retrieved entities by LLMs
before retrieving the subgraphs among these entities. It is worth mentioning that LLM-based
entity retrieval only works well for commonsense and fact-based KGs (e.g., Wikidata) rather than
domain-specific KGs, since the former KGs or their open text data forms (e.g., Wikipedia) might
have already been utilized to pre-train the LLMs. As a result, these KGs are well-known to LLMs,
while the domain-specific KGs may not be well-known to LLMs.
Vector-similarity based Entity Retrieval. This method leverages vector similarity search to
retrieve the relevant entities and relations from the KG that are relevant to the schema matching
questions. By representing both the questions and the knowledge graph components as dense vector
embeddings, the vector search techniques are used to identify the top-𝑘 relevant entities based on
efficient computation of similarity scores. This approach ensures high-quality and scalable retrieval
of knowledge graph components, making it well-suited for applications in schema matching and
semantic search.
Offline KG embedding and vector storage. The embeddings for KG entities and relations are gener-
ated in an offline manner using pre-trained transformer-based language models such as RoBERTa [36],
as it demonstrated strong results for vector search in terms of both effectiveness and computa-
tional efficiency [46]. These embeddings, along with associated metadata (e.g., entity or relation
identifiers), are stored in a vector database such as ChromaDB [50]. The storage process includes
indexing within the vector database to facilitate efficient retrieval of relevant embeddings during
online querying.
Online question embedding. The online component starts by generating embeddings for each ques-
tion. In particular, question embeddings are generated using Sentence-BERT [55], which employs
sections.content: 8 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár the same pre-trained model, RoBERTa, and is specifically designed for sentence embeddings because it is good at capturing the semantic meaning of sentences. This approach works for all KGs, including domain-specific ones, because sentence transformers, such as RoBERTa, are pre-trained on diverse datasets, enabling them to capture general semantic patterns and relationships. By embedding entities and relationships into universal vector space, they ensure that semantic similarity is preserved across domains. Online vector search. To retrieve the top-𝑘 most similar entities and relationships, we employ cosine similarity as the distance metric. Cosine similarity is chosen after extensive experimentation against alternative distance metrics such as Euclidean and Manhattan distances. Although Euclidean and Manhattan distances are effective for capturing absolute differences in vector space, cosine similarity is superior in our context as it measures the angular alignment between vectors, disregarding their magnitude. We experimentally observe that cosine similarity consistently outperforms other metrics in our vector-based search and retrieval. Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, and it is defined as: Cosine Similarity(𝐴, 𝐵) = 𝐴 𝐵 𝐴𝐵 Here, 𝐴 and 𝐵 represent the embeddings of the question and KG entity or relationship, respectively, denotes the dot product, and represents the magnitude of vector. Additionally, we use the HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) indexes implemented in the vector databases for efficient vector retrieval [44]. The HNSW index constructs graphbased structure where nodes represent data points, and edges connect neighboring points based on similarity, from which the search starts at high-level entry point and navigates through progressively denser graph layers, effectively narrowing down to the most similar neighbors. These optimizations ensure fast and scalable ANN searches, even for large datasets, which are necessary for scaling the system over large knowledge graphs such as Wikidata, where there are billions of entities and triples.

sections.title:
3.2.2 Retrieving Relevant Subgraphs from the KG. This module aims to retrieve relevant subgraphs,
paths, or triples from large KGs that contain concise knowledge to augment the generation capability
of LLMs for knowledge-intensive tasks. To fully leverage the rich semantic knowledge of KGs for
augmenting LLMs, we retrieve relevant subgraphs from large KGs by using one of the following
techniques. Among them, LLM-based subgraph retrieval, vector-based KG triple retrieval, and
hybrid subgraph retrieval aim to directly identify the relevant subgraphs from the KG. Only
BFS-based subgraph retrieval requires relevant entities retrieved from the previous phase (§3.2.1).
LLM-based Subgraph Retrieval. In this method, we call the LLMs to directly retrieve the relevant
subgraphs or paths that are relevant to answer the given question, without the previous step of
identifying relevant entities first. The prompts in Appendix A.3, including few-shot examples with
expected responses, are given to guide LLMs towards directly retrieving the relevant subgraphs
from large-scale KGs. Similar to previous cases, there is a placeholder {question} that will be replaced
with the real questions from our selected dataset in the prompt.
sections.content: Due to the fact that LLMs hallucinate and may also not know the KGs well, especially domainspecific KGs, the quality of the subgraphs retrieved by LLMs can often be poor. Similar to the LLM-based entity retrieval, the quality of the subgraphs retrieved by LLMs largely depends on the extent to which LLMs know the KGs. Since the commonsense and fact-based KGs or their open textual data forms might have already been utilized to pre-train LLMs, LLM-based subgraph retrieval works well for commonsense and fact-based KGs, while it might not work for domain-specific KGs. Vector-based KG Triple Retrieval. In this method, we focus on generating, storing, and retrieving embeddings for triples in large-scale knowledge graphs to facilitate vector similarity-based KG Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching 9 triple retrieval. First, the embeddings for KG entities and relationships are created by processing their labels and descriptions, fetched through the Wikidata API. These embeddings are generated using pre-trained language model, e.g., RoBERTa. The embeddings are then normalized to unit vectors to enhance the efficiency of cosine similarity computations. The embeddings, along with metadata such as entity and relationship identifiers, are stored in vector database. KG triple retrieval is performed by computing cosine similarity between the question embedding and the KG triple embeddings, identifying the top-𝑘 most relevant triples. BFS-based Subgraph Retrieval. After retrieving the relevant entities from large-scale KGs by leveraging either LLM-based entity retrieval or vector similarity-based entity retrieval, we explore the relevant subgraphs induced by these entities with the Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithm. Given set of retrieved entities 𝐸 = {𝑒1, 𝑒2, . . . , 𝑒𝑛 } from KG, the retrieval strategy depends on 𝑛. When 𝑛 = 1, local BFS expands the neighborhood of the single seed entity up to three hops. When 𝑛 2, we form entity pairs 𝑒𝑝 = {𝑒𝑠, 𝑒𝑒 } EP by combining the entities in 𝐸, where 𝑒𝑠 is the start entity and 𝑒𝑒 is the end entity, and retrieve the subgraphs of up to three hops connecting 𝑒𝑠 and 𝑒𝑒 (if any) via BFS. The three-hop search is trade-off solution between the number of retrieved subgraphs for subgraph refinement and the time complexity and the quality of the retrieved subgraphs based on our empirical results. The BFS-based subgraph retrieval supports two BFS pipelines:(1) local BFS in memory, and (2) remote BFS via SPARQL queries. The remote pipeline forms entity pairs in the same way as the local one. For each pair, it sends SPARQL query to Wikidata that searches for paths of up to three hops between 𝑒𝑠 and 𝑒𝑒 . The queries are generated from predefined templates (see Appendix A.6): the start and end entity identifiers are substituted into the template, intermediate entities and relations are left as variables, and UNION clauses cover both edge directions. The retrieved subgraphs are then refined with the same ranking scheme as in local BFS.

sections.title:
3.2.3 Ranking-based Retrieval Refinement. Our methodology incorporates several ranking schemes
to prioritize and rank the already retrieved paths from a knowledge graph. These schemes are
designed to select the most relevant paths, ensuring that only the best candidates are integrated.
This facilitates effective integration with LLMs by evaluating the retrieved paths based on the
ranking of relevance and structural significance.
sections.content: One ranking scheme is frequency-based ranking, which prioritizes those paths that also contain several of the top-𝑘 retrieved relations (3.2.1: Vector-similarity-based Entity Retrieval). Recall that the top-𝑘 retrieved relations are identified based on the similarity scores calculated between the question embedding and the relation embedding. To further enhance the relevance of retrieved paths, we employ second ranking strategy that normalizes frequency-based scoring with respect to path length. This normalization ensures that longer paths, which inherently consist of more relations, do not disproportionately dominate the rankings. This strategy ensures that paths are ranked based on both the presence of relevant relations and structural conciseness. Additionally, for 3.2.2: Vector-based KG Triple Retrieval, we directly use the cosine similarity between the question embedding and the triple embeddings to rank the retrieved triples. Based on our ranking scheme, we select the top-1, top-2, or all retrieved paths/triples to augment the large language model. Our experimental results show that using the top-2 or top-1 retrieved paths/triples is generally more effective and efficient in terms of LLMs retrieval-augmented generation compared to using all retrieved paths/triples.

sections.title:
3.2.4 Enhancing Prompts with Retrieved Subgraphs. After retrieving the relevant subgraphs from
external KGs, we leverage them as the semantic knowledge context to enhance the prompts of LLMs
for augmenting the generation of the final responses for schema matching tasks. To make LLMs
fully understand the retrieved subgraph, there is an option to convert the retrieved subgraph to
sections.content: 10 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár full text by introducing the verbalizer [78]. Namely, the LLMs can serve as the verbalizer, in which case the retrieved subgraphs will be converted to text by calling the LLMs again. However, this option is not necessary and not the optimal solution either, since the precondition of calling LLMs to convert the subgraph to text is that the LLMs can fully understand it. Besides, some structured knowledge of the retrieved subgraphs will be lost during the conversion from triples to text. In our case, each retrieved subgraph is semi-structured text with some special characters, such as arrows and operators, to represent multi-hop relations and separate multiple paths, which can still be understood and fully leveraged by LLMs. We feed the retrieved subgraphs within the prompts to LLMs directly and highlight the roles of the provided KG context with few-shot examples. The prompts, including the few-shot examples and the retrieved subgraphs from KGs to guide and augment LLMs in making the correct decisions, are demonstrated in the Appendix A.4. As shown in the prompt, we provide examples with explanations to guide LLMs to fully leverage the provided KG context when making decisions and generating final answers for schema-matching questions in our given examples. There are two placeholders, {question} and {paths}, that will be replaced with the real questions and the retrieved subgraphs from the selected dataset. Other placeholders [d1] and [d2] are descriptions for attribute1 and attribute2, respectively. It is worth mentioning that the KG context given in example 1 within the prompts provides extra knowledge about the attributes. Namely, the date of death is the opposite of the date of birth, which indicates that date of death and date of birth are not semantically equivalent even if they are syntactically similar. This precise knowledge provides the exact relationships between two matching attribute pairs, which is helpful for LLMs to generate the correct answers for the given schema matching questions.

sections.title:
3.2.5 Poorly-relevant Subgraphs Exclusion. One challenge in augmenting LLMs with retrieved
subgraphs from KG lies in the inclusion of irrelevant subgraphs that can mislead the model and
result in erroneous outputs. Although the ranking-based retrieval refinement designed in §3.2.3
can filter out the irrelevant subgraphs based on the vector similarity score, some poorly relevant
subgraphs may still exist in the refined results. The previous study [67] reveals that irrelevant
context significantly hampers RAG performance in knowledge-intensive tasks, highlighting the
critical importance of retrieving relevant and useful context for optimal results.
sections.content: Inspired by this, we introduce rule-based instruction tuning strategy to further exclude poorly relevant subgraphs from the previously retrieved and ranked subgraphs and mitigate the LLMs hallucinations. As shown in the prompt, we design an instruction to prompt (detailed in Appendix A.5) LLMs with examples in the manner of few-shot learning, which aims to guide LLMs to analyze the given schema matching question step by step and alleviate hallucinations by excluding the poorly relevant subgraph when making the decision. In particular, we instruct the LLM to assign relevance score between 0 and 10 to each given schema matching question and the provided retrieved subgraph from the external KG, based on few-shot examples with the assigned relevance score and explanation for scoring. We prompt and guide LLMs to only consider the provided and retrieved knowledge graph context if the relevance score is greater than or equal to 7, thereby filtering out distracting, poorly relevant subgraphs and ensuring that only high-value triples augment the model for schema matching. It is worth noting that the rule-based instruction tuning for poorly relevant subgraph exclusion in 3.2.5 is by default disabled in KG-RAG4SM in the main evaluation, unless otherwise stated, because it was intentionally designed for KG-RAG4SM with domain-specific KG. In 4.4.2, we provide experimental results on how instruction-tuning performs for improving the truthfulness of KG-RAG4SM even in the presence of retrieved poorly relevant subgraphs. sections.title:
4 Experimental Results
We empirically evaluate the performance of the proposed KG-RAG4SM method by comparing it
against the state-of-the-art schema matching approaches from two domains: pre-trained language
models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs). We conduct experiments using three widely used
schema matching benchmark datasets and a self-created dataset from the real-world healthcare
database. To evaluate the cross-domain transferability of KG-RAG4SM, we additionally include
two non-healthcare datasets, Bank and IMSA. Our code and datasets are available at Github1.
sections.content: We aim to investigate the following research questions. Exp-1: Effectiveness. How does our method compare with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) models for schema matching in terms of effectiveness? Exp-2: Efficiency. How does our method compare with the SOTA models for schema matching in terms of efficiency? Abl-1: Subgraph Retrieval. Which subgraph retrieval techniques work better for KG-RAG4SM in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency to generate high-quality results for schema matching? Abl-2: Backbone LLMs. Which LLMs perform better in KG-RAG4SM, e.g., do fewer-parameter LLMs work better than large-size LLMs for KG-RAG4SM? Ext-1: Scalability across KG Domains. Which KGs work better in KG-RAG4SM, e.g., do domain-specific KGs work better than commonsense KGs for KG-RAG4SM? Ext-2: Truthfulness of KG-RAG4SM. Does the rule-based relevance scoring and instructiontuning work for improving the truthfulness of KG-RAG4SM? Ext-3: Ablation Study on Subgraph Refinement in KG-RAG4SM and Comparison with SOTA GraphRAG. We investigate the following two research questions: (Ext-3a) What is the isolated contribution of the similarity ranking-based subgraph refinement mechanism to the performance of KG-RAG4SM? (Ext-3b) How does the complete KG-RAG4SM framework perform relative to the state-of-the-art GraphRAG baseline? Case: Hallucinations. How does KG-RAG4SM mitigate the hallucinations of LLMs for complex schema matching in real-world scenario?

(TP) + False Negative (FN)). F1 score is a balance between precision and recall.

the domain of KGs from commonsense KGs (Wikidata) to domain-specific KGs (Medical KGs) and
evaluate the effectiveness of medical KGs in KG-RAG4SM. In view of our schema matching dataset
originating from the healthcare databases, we retrieve and rank the relevant entities from the UMLS
KG based on vector similarity and then expand each entity with retrieved relations from the UMLS
KG by using the UMLS API20 to form the triples. Specifically, we leverage UMLS-BERT [45] to
encode the given schema matching question and then query the relevant entities from UMLS, and
next retrieve the relation for each entity by using the caching mechanism to accelerate relation
retrieval from UMLS API endpoints. For each entity, we expand it with queried relations as triples
and then rank the triples based on the similarity score between the question and the entity. We
present results of KG-RAG4SM with GPT-4o-mini and Jellyfish-8B as backbone LLMs and the

etc.) from source and target data models, are more relevant to the entities and taxonomic

and relations (e.g., diabetes status: Prid: Pt: ˆ Patient: Nom, has_supersystem, patient,
etc.) from medical KGs. Most of the triples that exist in UMLS KG are one-hop relations, as the UMLS
maintains the entities and their associated one-hop relations, while the multiple-hop relations are

(2) Answers Prone to False Positives: Similar to other RAG systems, Graph RAG and KG-RAG systems can be easily distracted by irrelevant context [62] and are prone to generating false positive answers with ambiguous or poorly relevant KG context. In particular, the results get worse when it comes to the lower relevance and quality of the retrieved KG triples, such as triples retrieved from the UMLS KG in our schema matching case. For instance, the KG triples from the UMLS KG show the connections between stopping medication and drug exposure, and the LLMs incorrectly infer that the reason for stopping medication is associated with drug exposure. However, the retrieved connections explicitly mention that stopping medication (120234) is synonym of Medication discontinued (274512008), which is associated with Drug therapy (416608005), but Drug therapy (416608005) is subclass of Drug or medicament (410942007) rather than semantically equivalent relation. Since LLMs are prone to generating false positive answers based on the found connections from the provided KG context, this further induces decreased performance of KG-RAG4SM in this scenario. Notice that we have not employed rule-based relevance scoring and instruction tuning (3.2.5) in this experiment, and we demonstrate this modules impact separately later in 4.4.2.

sections.title:
5 Related Work
Schema Matching and Data Integration. Schema matching is a process of establishing semantic
associations between different schemata, in which the semantic correspondences between the source
and target schemas are usually identified [54]. In contrast to schema matching, schema mapping is
a process of generating the assertions and mappings from the identified semantic correspondence,
by which the source schema can be mapped onto the target schema to provide a common interface
for accessing and querying heterogeneous data [17]. In general, the correspondences between
the source and target schemas can be identified manually by domain experts, which requires a
lot of human effort and experience [41]. In the case of manual mapping, mismatches and errors
are also inevitable, as the intensive and repeated work might distract humans. To improve the
matching efficiency and to minimize mismatches, an auto-match system is designed to support
automatic schema matching based on machine learning [2]. In this method, probability knowledge
is obtained from domain experts based on Bayesian learning, which provides an attribute dictionary
to find optimal matching pairs. Considering the strengths of similarity-based matching and machine
learning-based matching, a hybrid schema matching model is proposed by combining lexical and
semantic similarity with machine learning [6].
sections.content: To free human hands from the tedious schema matching task, new semi-automatic schema matching approach is proposed [13]. In this approach, the domain ontologies and sample instances are reused to identify and determine the semantic correspondences between schemata. Similarly, background ontologies are utilized to provide the semantic reference for schema matching based on ontology alignment [48]. To minimize mismatches and errors, the medical knowledge bases from the medical encyclopedia are utilized to learn better representations of medical concepts and properties. Thereby, medical schema matching method is proposed based on the relation alignment between Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching 29 the description embedding of an extracted medical entity and learned heterogeneous knowledge graph embedding [18]. However, these methods follow supervised learning, in which large labeled data are required for model training. Recently, several schema matching approaches based on LLMs have been proposed to address the above limitations, such as fine-tuned LLMs Magneto [37], retrieval-enhanced LLMs [60], and reasoning-guided LLMs [79]. To improve the performance of LLMs for data preprocessing, an instruction-tuning LLM [83] is proposed, which enables optional knowledge injection during inference through instruction tuning with reasoning based on domain knowledge. Since the inherent knowledge might be useful to enhance LLMs for schema matching, RAG-based approaches are proposed to augment LLMs by retrieving the relevant knowledge from text chunks constructed based on the textual descriptions of tables and attributes, e.g., retrieval-enhanced large language model for schema matching [60] that retrieves the top-𝑘 documents from the textual documents based on semantic relevance. Inspired by RAG on LLMs, compositional language model for schema matching [59] enhances and refines the results based on semantic retrieval from multivector documents and confidence scoring by multiple calls of LLMs. Similarly, an LLM-based knowledge-compliant schema and entity-matching framework [79] is proposed that guides LLM reasoning based on pseudo-code-based task decomposition and knowledge retrieval from domain knowledge sets by calling LLMs to query the relevant keywords. The prevailing methods of schema matching could be classified into five categories: similaritybased matching [2, 6, 34], graph-based matching [13], pre-training language model-based matching [18, 68, 88], LLMs-based matching [83], and RAG-based matching [59, 60, 79]. Although there are some recent works, such as ReMatch [60] and Matchmaker [59], they leverage RAG over LLMs to address schema matching, but only the knowledge from the textual documents of the descriptions for the table and attribute is retrieved for augmentation. KcMF [79] retrieves knowledge from the self-built knowledge set, but the knowledge from the large commonsense and fact-based KGs in the real world has not been adapted and fully leveraged to augment the LLMs for schema matching. To some extent, the aforementioned methods achieve (semi-) automatic schema matching, but they are still incapable of resolving the semantic ambiguities and conflicts in some complex mapping cases because of the missing evidence and factual knowledge. Besides schema matching and mapping, the field of data preparation/integration deals with several other critical challenges, e.g., data acquisition, extraction, cleaning, augmentation, transformation, and annotation; entity matching; ontology alignment; and data fusion, among others [3, 8, 12]. Recent advances in deep learning and foundation models have also achieved promising results on many such tasks. Notable works include deep learning embedding-based data integration over relational databases [7, 27], and ontology matching [26], pre-trained language models (PLMs) for entity matching [33, 66], and column type annotation [64], large language models (LLMs)- powered entity resolution [14, 30, 52] and other data wrangling tasks [47, 89], etc. The focus of our work is schema matching, which is different from the aforementioned problems. We do not consider cell values (nor rows/entities) in the table; instead, we directly aim at finding semantic correspondence among attribute names (i.e., column names) in tables from the source and target schema. Additionally, none of these works employ external and large-scale knowledge graph-based retrieval augmentation paradigms to enhance the LLMs performance in data integration tasks. Knowledge-augmented LLMs and RAG. There are several ways in which external knowledge from KGs can be integrated with LLMs [42]. To leverage the strengths and capabilities of hierarchical and structured knowledge in complex reasoning, the KGs and text are aligned and interact to jointly train the language models [82, 87] for knowledge-intensive tasks. In the phase of joint learning, the text and KG pair are aligned via entity linking and then fed into the cross-model encoder to bidirectionally fuse text and KG, thereby performing joint reasoning on text and KG. In 30 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár addition to joint learning, knowledge-based instruction tuning integrates graph representations into language generation by aligning LLM inference with the graphs topological structure, enabling more effective use of graph knowledge for complex reasoning [5]. However, the resulting model must be re-fine-tuned whenever the KG is updated or when adapting to new domain, because the method embeds only static KG information into the model parameters. Graph reasoning approaches such as RoG [38] and ToG [65] guide LLM inference using KGderived reasoning paths generated through BFS or beam search, rather than relying solely on static knowledge fusion. KG-CoT [90] extends this idea by introducing chain-of-thought reasoning over graphs, producing explicit reasoning paths and confidence scores based on transition matrices. Agent-based methods have also been explored, exemplified by KG-Agent [24], which treats the LLM as an agent that autonomously selects KG-related tools and updates memory for iterative reasoning. Despite their strengths, these graph reasoning methods repeatedly search paths at each step of beam search or CoT, resulting in substantial computational overhead on large-scale KGs. Different from the aforementioned techniques, RAG aims to retrieve relevant knowledge from specific data sources, such as text chunks, tabular data, graph data, etc., to augment the capability and reliability of LLMs for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks [29]. However, the mainstream RAG methods retrieve the relevant knowledge from the textual chunks, which ignore the structured information and inter-relations of these textual chunks. To mitigate this limitation, Graph RAG [22, 80] and KG-RAG [57] are proposed. Instead of retrieving knowledge from textual chunks, Graph RAG directly retrieves the relevant paths from the graph data. GraphRAG [22] retrieves subgraphs from the textual graph that is indexed based on PLMs and then integrates the retrieved and pruned subgraphs with the query by aggregating and aligning the graph embeddings with text vectors based on GNNs. Similarly, KG-based RAG aims to augment LLMs with KGs by leveraging the reasoning capability of knowledge from various knowledge sources for knowledge-intensive tasks. KG-RAG approaches retrieve the subgraph from the self-constructed KG based on unstructured text or textual chunks [57] or from the inherent KGs derived from the KGQA dataset [32] to augment the reasoning capability of LLMs for complex QA. Recent research works have demonstrated the remarkable performance of KG-RAG on several knowledge-intensive tasks such as text classification [71], sentiment analysis [31], entity linking [61], KGQA [32, 42, 57], recommendation [9], etc. These mainstream Graph RAG and KG-RAG approaches usually retrieve knowledge from local and small-sized graphs built from text chunks or the inherent KGs derived from the KGQA dataset. Our method differs from the existing KG-RAG on the KGQA; it leverages vector-based retrieval and graph traversal-based retrieval to retrieve the relevant subgraphs from large external KGs instead of constructed KGs based on textual chunks or the inherent KGs derived from the KGQA dataset. It mainly focuses on augmenting LLMs with KGs for complex schema matching tasks rather than the commonly investigated natural language processing and understanding tasks.

We investigated the scalability across KG domains from commonsense KG to domain-specific KG and the truthfulness of KGRAG4SM with poorly relevant retrieved KG context. Our case studies from real-world scenarios showed that the hallucination of LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our method. In this study, we augmented LLMs with relevant subgraphs retrieved from large external KG via few-shot learning. However, resolving knowledge conflicts between the internal knowledge of LLMs and the retrieved KG, examining retrieval performance across KGs varying in scale and connectivity, and developing more advanced graph traversal strategies to further optimize subgraph retrieval on large KGs remain interesting directions for future work. Additionally, we shall investigate how our KG-RAG paradigm can improve other LLM-based data integration and data fusion tasks. sections.content: B.1 Detailed Analysis of Domain-specific UMLS vs. Commonsense Wikidata KG We present examples of schema matching questions and their corresponding retrieved triples from UMLS KG and Wikidata KG in Table 14 and provide an additional comparison of KG triples. We observed that the UMLS KG triple provides more healthcare-technical specialized knowledge than the Wikidata KG, but it is not always useful for metadata-level schema matching. Although all of our schema matching datasets originate from healthcare databases, the questions of schemamatching pairs including table name (admission, patient, visit, insurance, service, etc.), attribute name (admission_location, patient_weight, visit_date, insurance_id, service_provider, etc.) from source and target data model; are more relevant to the entities and taxonomic relations (e.g., patient, instance of, human, etc.) from commonsense KGs rather than medical entities and relations (e.g, diabetes status:Prid: Pt: ˆ Patient:Nom, has_supersystem, patient, etc.) from domain-specific UMLS KGs. To further investigate this interesting finding, we manually selected 160 schema questions that cover more professional terms (e.g., drug_exposure, medications, immunization, etc.) in the healthcare domain from the Synthea dataset and compared the results of KG-RAG4SM with Jellyfish-8B and the top-2 ranked triples from UMLS and Wikidata KGs in Table 15. Figure 6a shows the confusion matrix of Jellyfish-8B on the EMED baseline. The reasons behind this are twofold: (1) the dataset is unseen, and (2) it is highly imbalanced. Detailed Analysis of SMAT Baseline with 100% Recall We present detailed results and discussion of the SMAT baseline, as we observed that SMAT achieved 100% recall across all datasets. Figure 6 shows the confusion matrix of the SMAT baseline, which demonstrates that SMAT tends to return positive answer and results in 100% recall. The confusion matrix shows that SMAT exhibits strong bias toward predicting the positive class, assigning positive labels to all matching pairs while failing to identify any negatives. Moreover, the dataset is highly imbalanced and negative-dominant, with only small fraction of positive pairs in the ground truth. As result, SMAT aggressively classifies negative samples as positive, capturing the few true positives but at the cost of substantial misclassification. In contrast, our proposed method achieves more balanced trade-off between recall and precision, leading to more robust schema-matching performance for data integration.

sections.content: C.1 Ablation Study on the Impact of Embedding Method To assess the effect of the embedding method on vector-based KG triple retrieval in KG-RAG4SM with Wikidata5M KG, we conduct an ablation study comparing our 768-dimensional RoBERTa-base embeddings with jina-embeddings-v3, state-of-the-art multilingual model with 512 dimensions. Table 16 summarizes the performance of KG-RAG4SM with different embedding models and GPT-4o-mini on the CMS dataset. The results demonstrate that KG-RAG4SM with RoBERTa-base consistently outperforms the version with jina-embeddings-v3, which indicates the strength of high-dimensional embedding method in our KG-RAG4SM. This suggests that higher-dimensional embeddings capture richer semantic information for vector retrieval, albeit at increased indexing and search cost. This also highlights that our RoBERTa-base is trade-off configuration to balance the performance and the computational cost of indexing and vector search for vector-based retrieval in KG-RAG4SM. 42 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár Table 16. To analyze the sensitivity of BFS search depth in KG-RAG4SM, we conduct new empirical study on the sensitivity of BFS search depth with settings of 2, 3, and 4 in KG-RAG4SM with GPT-4o-mini and Wikidata5M KG on the CMS dataset. Table 17 shows the results of KG-RAG4SM with different BFS search depths. Table 17. Sensitivity analysis of BFS search depth in KG-RAG4SM with GPT-4o-mini on CMS dataset. Metric (%) 3 Top-1 Ranked Top-1 Ranked Top-1 Ranked 4 F1 46.67 28.00 35.00 42.11 32.00 36.36 44.44 32.00 37. The results show that KG-RAG4SM with BFS search depth of 4 achieves the best F1 score, while BFS depth 3 yields comparable results to KG-RAG4SM with BFS depth 2. This highlights trend that increasing the depth from 2 to 3 and 4 results in an increase in the F1 score. However, the design choice of BFS search depth in KG-RAG4SM is determined by jointly considering overall matching performance (F1 score), retrieval time, token cost, and end-to-end latency. We justify our default design choice of BFS search depth of 3 as favorable accuracyefficiency trade-off in the following BFS search time evaluation. Remote BFS vs. BFS in Local Memory. We further evaluate KG-RAG4SM by comparing the number of retrieved paths and triples, along with the average BFS search time per question, across search depths of 2 to 4. The analysis considers both remote BFS via API and local BFS in-memory settings. Specifically, remote BFS search uses the full Wikidata KG through its SPARQL endpoint, whereas local in-memory BFS operates over the Wikidata5M. Since Wikidata5M contains only subset of the entities and relations in Wikidata, the two configurations do not necessarily provide the same graph connectivity or retrieved paths, even when using the same BFS depth. Consequently, the two configurations may retrieve different numbers of paths and triples. For the local in-memory implementation, the per-question BFS search times reported in Table 18 are distinct from the one-time graph preparation and process-initialization costs. The serialized Wikidata5M adjacency representation and entity/relation labels require 1.23 GB of local storage, while fresh-process initialization takes 57.90 on average over three runs, comprising 49.59 for loading the adjacency graph and 8.32 for loading the labels. Peak resident memory during initialization reaches 8.31 GB. We report the complete deployment footprint and initialization breakdown in Appendix D.2. Table 18 shows that increasing the BFS search depth leads to steep growth in retrieved triples and paths, as well as average BFS search time per question, both in remote BFS search via API and local BFS search in memory. As shown in Table 18, at BFS depth of three, remote retrieval produces Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching 43 Table 18. Comparison of the number of retrieved paths, triples, and average BFS search time per question with remote and local BFS implementations varying in search depth. The difference becomes more pronounced at depth four, where remote retrieval obtains 17.83 paths and 63.76 triples, compared with 13.34 paths and 48.07 triples locally. These observations are consistent with the broader graph connectivity available through fullscale Wikidata, which can expose additional intermediate entities and semantic relationships not represented in Wikidata5M. These results also demonstrate that BFS depth of 3 offers favorable accuracyefficiency trade-off for KG-RAG4SM in both remote API-based and local in-memory search settings. It provides richer retrieval, covering substantially more multi-hop paths than depth 2, while maintaining lower search time and end-to-end latency, and avoiding the excessive delays and timeout risks observed at depth 4. This trade-off between traversal depth, retrieved knowledge coverage, and search latency is fundamental consideration when deploying BFS-based retrieval over large-scale knowledge graphs such as Wikidata5M, as broader coverage often introduces noisy information that degrades overall performance. The results also demonstrate that KG-RAG4SM with local BFS search in memory is always faster than remote BFS search via the Wikidata API, which further confirms the deployment flexibility of KG-RAG4SM with local in-memory BFS strategy in real-world data integration scenarios. sections.content: To analyze the sensitivity of the relevance score threshold in instruction tuning-based knowledge exclusion, we conduct new empirical study on the relevance score threshold with settings of 3, 5, 7, and 9 in KG-RAG4SM with Jellyfish-8B and UMLS KGs on the Synthea dataset. Table 19 shows the results of KG-RAG4SM with different settings of the relevance score threshold in instruction tuning-based knowledge exclusion. Table 19. Sensitivity analysis of relevance score threshold in IT-based knowledge exclusion of KG-RAG4SM with Jellyfish-8B and UMLS KGs on the Synthea dataset. Metric (%) 3 5 9 Top-2 Ranked Top-2 Ranked Top-2 Ranked Top-2 Ranked F1 21.43 27.27 24.00 23.08 27.27 25.00 33.33 45.45 38. 21.43 27.27 24.00 We observed that the and F1 increase as the relevance score threshold rises from 3 to 7, but performance declines when the threshold is further increased from 7 to 9. This is mainly because increasing the relevance threshold from 3 to 7 filters out less relevant or noisy knowledge and 44 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár improves performance, but raising it further to 9 becomes too strict for knowledge exclusion. This confirms the effectiveness of our designed instruction-tuning-based knowledge exclusion in excluding weakly relevant or noisy knowledge without discarding relevant and useful knowledge for reasoning. These results further indicate that threshold of 7 provides balance between retaining relevant knowledge and excluding noise. More broadly, the analysis demonstrates that the relevance threshold is key parameter in instruction tuning-based knowledge exclusion, enabling effective filtering of irrelevant triples when set appropriately. C.4 LLM-based Subgraph Retrieval In LLM-based KG retrieval, we treat the LLM as natural language interface for the commonsense KG. This is mainly based on the fact that commonsense KGs, such as Wikidata, are well known to LLMs, as the commonsense KGs or their open textual data forms might have already been utilized to pre-train LLMs. Accordingly, we designed an LLM-based entity retrieval + BFS and an LLM-based subgraph retrieval. In the LLM-based entity retrieval + BFS, the interaction pipeline is summarized as: (1) Entity/Relation ID Generation: The LLM is prompted to output the Wikidata entity identifier (QID) and relation identifier (PID) that are relevant to the given schema matching question in context learning; (2) ID fetcher and Verification: We verify and fetch the name of the entity and the relation with the identifier from Wikidata via the Wikidata REST API; (3) Subgraph Search: We execute the subgraph search via BFS with the verified entity and relation. In LLM-based subgraph retrieval, the interaction pipeline is summarized as: (1) Path Generation: The LLM is prompted to output the paths from Wikidata that are relevant to the given schemamatching question; (2) ID fetcher and Verification: We verify the paths by fetching the name of the entity and relation with identifiers from Wikidata via the Wikidata REST API. Our empirical evaluation (Abl-1: subgraph retrieval) results reveal that the LLM-based subgraph retrieval method works on commonsense KGs because LLMs know the concepts and relations of Wikidata, but sometimes it returns the entity and relation identifiers that actually do not exist in Wikidata. However, LLM-based subgraph retrieval works for commonsense KGs, whereas it may not work as effectively for domain-specific KGs, as LLMs are not familiar with them. C.5 KG-RAG4SM with Domain KGs vs. LLM-based Schema Matching To highlight the contribution of retrieved external knowledge rather than the LLMs internal parametric knowledge, we compare KG-RAG4SM using the domain-specific UMLS KG against LLM-based schema matching with the same backbone models under low-overlap setting  (Table 20)  . The results show that KG-RAG4SM with UMLS consistently outperforms the LLM-only baseline Table 20. KG-RAG4SM with Jellyfish-8B and UMLS KGs vs. LLM-based SM on Synthea dataset. Metric (%) KG-RAG4SM With Rule-based IT Top-1 Ranked Top-2 Ranked LLM-based SM F1 35.71 45.45 40.00 33.33 45.45 38. 10.52 36.36 16.32 across all metrics. This confirms that the performance gains stem from the retrieved external knowledge, rule-based instruction tuning, and structural grounding, rather than from the LLMs inherent parameter knowledge. Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching 45 C.6 Qualitative Analysis on Improvement To qualitatively illustrate the impact of retrieved subgraphs in KG-RAG4SM, we present the confusion matrices (TP, FN, FP, TN) for KG-RAG4SM using Jellyfish-8B as the backbone LLM with top-1 triples retrieved via vector-based entity retrieval plus BFS search, compared with the LLM baseline on the CMS dataset. As shown in Figure 7, KG-RAG4SM achieves 2,529 TN and 9 FP, whereas the LLM-only baseline yields 2,524 TN and 14 FP. This demonstrates that incorporating Fig. 7. Confusion matrix of LLM-based schema matching and KG-RAG4SM on CMS dataset. the retrieved subgraph increases TN and reduces FP without decreasing TP or increasing FN. The reduction in FP indicates that the external KG subgraph provides structural factual context that enables more reliable reasoning, allowing KG-RAG4SM to generate correct answers on complex schema-matching cases. These findings are further supported by the case study in 4.5, which shows that the structural knowledge contained in the retrieved subgraph enhances the LLMs reasoning ability in complex schema-matching scenarios and reduces hallucinations during matching.

sections.title: D Complexity and the Additional Cost Efficiency Analysis
sections.content: D.1 Complexity Analysis and Empirical Verification We provide time complexity analysis of vector retrieval and BFS graph traversal, along with empirical verification of the computational feasibility of KG-RAG4SM on large-scale KGs. Time Complexity Analysis. Let 𝐺 = (𝑉 , 𝐸) denote KG, where 𝑉 is set of entities with 𝑛 = 𝑉 and 𝐸 is set of edges with 𝑚 = 𝐸. The average branching factor is the average out-degree of node in the KG: 𝑏 = 𝑚/𝑛. For given query 𝑞, the complexity is derived as follows: (1) Vector Retrieval: For cosine similarity search over KG embeddings in dimension 𝑑 vector space, the time complexity scales linearly with the KG size 𝑛: 𝑂 (𝑛 𝑑). In practice, Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes such as HNSW can reduce query cost substantially, often exhibiting sublinear empirical search behavior: 𝑂 (log 𝑛 𝑑), although worst-case complexity depends on the index and data distribution. (2) BFS Traversal: Unlike standard BFS that may visit all nodes 𝑂 (𝑉 + 𝐸) for each entity, our designed BFS search is constrained by the number of entity pairs formed based on the number of seed entities 𝑉𝑆 in the initial vector-based entity retrieval and the maximum BFS search depth 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 . The BFS search executes for each entity pair, so the total time complexity for the graph traversal phase in the worst case expands exponentially with depth 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 is: 𝑂 (𝑉𝑆 2 𝑏𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 ). Therefore, the time complexity of the subgraph retrieval is 𝑂 (log 𝑛 𝑑 + 𝑉𝑆 2 𝑏𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 ), which is dominated by the maximum BFS search depth 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 and the local connectivity of the KG, and is not directly determined by the overall number of entities in the KG. 46 Chuangtao Ma, Sriom Chakrabarti, Arijit Khan, and Bálint Molnár Empirical Analysis and Feasibility Verification. Since the above complexity analysis indicates that the time complexity of KG retrieval in KG-RAG4SM depends primarily on 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 and the local connectivity of the KG rather than the KG size, our empirical analysis focuses on the BFS traversal depth (𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 ) instead of the KG scale. To evaluate the impact of BFS depth (𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 ), we compare remote traversal over full-scale Wikidata with local in-memory traversal over Wikidata5M (𝑛 4.6𝑀, 𝑚 20.6𝑀). Table 18 reports the number of retrieved paths and triples, alongside the average search time per question, as the BFS search depth 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 varies from 2 to 4. Specifically, as shown in Table 18, increasing the depth for remote full-Wikidata BFS, from 3 to 4, results in 7 increase in retrieved triples and causes the average search time to reach 98.45 seconds per query. These results indicate that increasing the BFS search depth 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 significantly increases the number of retrieved triples, but also incurs higher BFS search latency and greater risk of API timeouts. This suggests that trade-off between BFS search depth and search time is necessary to balance the number of retrieved triples with search time when adapting to large-scale KGs. D.2 Graph Retrieval and Deployment Efficiency Retrieval Latency and Runtime Analysis. To further evaluate the efficiency and feasibility of KG-RAG4SM on large-scale KG, we analyze the vector search runtime and BFS retrieval latency of our KG-RAG4SM. We also provide BFS search latency optimization strategy for practical system deployment of KG-RAG4SM by extending BFS from remote search via Wikidata endpoint (full Wikidata KG) access to local BFS search in memory (Wikidata5M). We measure the runtime of vector search and BFS graph traversal, both in remote search and local memory search, on the CMS dataset, and then report the average retrieval latency per question. The latency is divided into the initial vector search and the graph traversal. Table 21. End-to-end latency of vector-based entity retrieval + BFS subgraph retrieval on CMS dataset. Latency Breakdown (Sec) Remote BFS via API BFS in Local Memory Retrieval Latency - Vector Search - BFS Graph Traversal 83.77 0.0001 83.7729 5.47 0.0001 5.4690 As summarized in Table 21, the vector search stage averages approximately 0.0001 seconds per question. The BFS graph traversal stage is the most time-consuming phase, as it involves retrieving relational paths from the large-scale KG. The average latency per question is 83.77 and 5.47 s, under the settings of remote BFS search over full-scale Wikidata through its SPARQL endpoint and local in-memory BFS search over Wikidata5M, respectively, with maximum BFS search depth 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 = 3. Specifically, KG-RAG4SM with in-memory BFS search achieves approximately 15 reduction in retrieval latency compared to remote BFS search over full-scale Wikidata. This is mainly because remote BFS involves network communication and query processing through the Wikidata SPARQL endpoint, whereas local BFS directly traverses the in-memory Wikidata5M graph. Moreover, since Wikidata5M contains only subset of the entities and relations in full-scale Wikidata, differences in graph coverage may also affect the number of retrieved paths and triples. Therefore, the observed latency difference reflects both the retrieval implementations and the underlying graph configurations, rather than comparison over identical graphs. These results demonstrate that the local in-memory BFS strategy is computationally efficient and deployable under realistic implementation settings. We also observe significant trend: as the search depth increases, the number of retrieved triples grows rapidly, directly impacting retrieval and graph traversal cost. Based on the sensitivity analysis Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching 47 results in Table 17 and Table 18, BFS search depth of 𝐷𝑚𝑎𝑥 = 3 offers favorable balance between factual grounding and computational efficiency, providing sufficient contextual factual knowledge to ground the LLMs inference without incurring prohibitive latency or timeout risks. Although the end-to-end retrieval latency is dominated by the graph traversal stage, our theoretical and empirical analysis demonstrates the practical feasibility and computational efficiency of KG-RAG4SM using Wikidata5M for local BFS and full-scale Wikidata for remote BFS, with balanced BFS search depth. Local Deployment and Initialization Cost. To further assess the practical deployment requirements of the local in-memory BFS implementation, we report its storage footprint, graph loading and construction cost, and hardware requirements in Table 22. Table 22. Deployment cost and hardware requirements of the local in-memory BFS implementation on Wikidata5M. Constructing the serialized adjacency cache is one-time preprocessing operation requiring 111.97 s, while loading the graph in fresh process takes 49.59 on average over three runs. No separate graph index or GPU is employed for local BFS traversal. Overall, by implementing BFS search in local memory, KG-RAG4SM achieves acceptable latency for real-world applications, highlighting its deployment flexibility in schema matching. However, systematic empirical evaluation of subgraph retrieval across KGs varying in scale and topological density is beyond the scope of this work. Developing more advanced graph traversal strategies to further optimize subgraph retrieval on large KGs remains important for future investigation.
